overview: Martinique’s history spans a plantation colony and a continuing Caribbean society within France. Writers and musicians developed distinctive cultural forms. Its separate map intervals do not represent an unchanged government.

periods.title: Anse Trabaud’s changing coastal settlement
periods.summary: Excavations reveal pottery and unusually well-preserved plant remains beneath coastal deposits. Researchers reconstruct settlement beside a shoreline that changed over time.

periods.title: French colonial settlement
periods.summary: A French settlement was established in 1635. Colonial administration subsequently combined a governor with an intendant, while enslaved labour sustained the plantation order.

periods.title: British occupation
periods.summary: British forces occupied Martinique in 1762 during imperial warfare. The island returned to French control the following year.

periods.title: French colonial administration resumes
periods.summary: Martinique became the seat of the French government of the Windward Islands after its return to France.

periods.title: Occupation leaves slavery intact
periods.summary: During British occupation, the French abolition decree of 1794 was not applied in Martinique.

periods.title: Slavery continues after the return to France
periods.summary: France’s recovery of the island in 1802 preserved slavery rather than restoring freedom already achieved there. Further political changes did not end the institution before 1848.

periods.title: Uprising and emancipation
periods.summary: Revolt on 22 May helped force the local abolition proclamation of 23 May, before the Paris decree officially reached the island. Enslaved people acted in securing their own freedom.

periods.title: Mount Pelée’s eruption transforms Saint-Pierre
periods.summary: The eruption destroyed Saint-Pierre on 8 May 1902 and killed thousands. The eruptive episode also became a defining case in the development of volcanology.

periods.title: Tropiques creates a literary forum
periods.summary: Aimé and Suzanne Césaire, René Ménil and collaborators published a journal connecting Caribbean experience with poetry, philosophy and criticism, despite wartime censorship.

periods.title: Departmental status
periods.summary: The law of 19 March 1946 made Martinique a French overseas department, replacing its colonial administrative status.

periods.title: Combined territorial institutions
periods.summary: The territorial collectivity’s institutions were installed in December 2015, bringing together responsibilities previously exercised by the general and regional councils within France.

sections.title: Discoveries beneath the shore and town

items.text: At Anse Trabaud in Sainte-Anne, excavators recovered wood, seeds and probable calabash fragments from deeply buried coastal deposits. These fragile materials add evidence that ordinary pottery assemblages cannot supply. The report describes exceptionally good preservation, while treating several botanical identifications as preliminary.

Manchineel stones in one sediment sample suggest a coastal environment where the poisonous tree grew. They are not evidence that people ate its fruit. Together with the sequence of sand and organic deposits, plant remains help reconstruct the changing surroundings in which the village’s inhabitants lived.

Saint-Pierre’s port area preserved stacks of imported porcelain and earthenware sealed by the 1902 disaster. Researchers identified heat-marked impressions of straw used as packing. Plates that had been stored for sale therefore reveal both overseas supply and the practical work of transporting fragile goods.

The same ceramics research distinguishes imported tableware from locally made water vessels and industrial pottery. Sugar moulds, molasses pots and roof tiles served different tasks from cups and plates. Marks and clay types help investigate workshops, although several proposed manufacturing places remain tentative.

Plantation slavery survived the changes of imperial control around 1800. When France recovered Martinique in 1802, the incoming administration maintained an existing system of coercion. The island’s chronology therefore differs from that of colonies where the 1794 abolition had actually taken effect.

The events of May 1848 involved enslaved workers at Le Prêcheur, Morne-Rouge and Saint-Pierre. Their mobilization and the ensuing violence forced an early local proclamation of abolition. The distinction between the uprising on 22 May and the decree on 23 May makes the participants’ agency visible.

Freedom left difficult questions about land and work unresolved. Compensation was eventually arranged for those claiming losses from emancipation, while formerly enslaved people received none. Abolition ended legal enslavement but did not itself create equal access to property.
Copies of parish and civil registers were collected to safeguard legal rights and administration. These records let researchers follow particular households through births, marriages and deaths.

Tropiques began in 1941 through collaboration among teachers and writers including Aimé and Suzanne Césaire and René Ménil. Its essays and poetry treated Caribbean experience as a subject of intellectual creation. Literary scholar Olga Hel-Bongo explains how apparently cultural subjects could carry criticism of colonial authority.

Suzanne Césaire helped bring manuscripts to the censorship authorities. The journal’s contributors used indirection as well as open argument; censorship interrupted publication in 1943. Their achievement involved editing, securing print and reaching readers under pressure, alongside the writing itself.

The community association AM4 describes the tibwa as two dry hardwood sticks that maintain a repeating rhythm, struck against a drum’s rear or sometimes bamboo. The bèlè drum uses a wooden barrel body and an animal-skin head; the player sits astride it and works with hands and heel.

Singing moves between a lead voice and a responding chorus. Instrument combinations vary by region and kind of music, so one ensemble cannot represent every Martinican practice. The tradition depends on shared timing, remembered verses and skilled interaction as much as on the construction of instruments.

In 1946, Césaire presented a parliamentary report supporting departmental status. The record of his interventions also includes food supply, protections for agricultural workers and bringing unused land into cultivation. These questions connect constitutional change with the daily concerns of households and labourers.

The 1902 catastrophe gave the Pelean eruptive type its name and helped scientists understand violent volcanic processes. The forests and volcanoes of northern Martinique entered UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2023 for their geological and ecological importance. Recognition preserves both scientific evidence and places inseparable from local memory.

ending.text: Colonial administration gave way to departmental status in 1946. Territorial institutions changed again in 2015, within France. Martinican society continues across these changes.
